stem: Invented for practice. A toy passes marks A, B and C at steady beats. The marks have equal gaps. Mark its next place and say what repeats.
answer: One equal gap beyond C; equal gaps at equal beats.
steps: One equal gap beyond C. | Cite the repeating gap.
samples: One equal gap beyond C, because each beat covers the same gap. | The next mark stays at C.

stem: Watch the marble and cup. What changes do you notice? What possible cause should we test?
answer: Describe visible cup travel or sound; suggest a tentative cause.
steps: Separate what was observed from a possible cause. | Accept plausible ideas without energy words.
samples: The cup went farther; maybe approach speed mattered. | My guess proves every result.

stem: Record one observation from the rolls. Add one question for another trial.
answer: An observed change and a repeatable question, kept distinct.
steps: Observation describes something seen. | Question could be checked by another trial.
samples: The cup moved. Will a repeated faster roll move it farther? | I observed what tomorrow will do.

stem: The pictures show two train speeds. Draw your possible explanation for the tower's different changes. Add one question that could test your idea.
answer: Tentatively connect train motion to displaced pieces; ask a testable question.
steps: Drawing gives a plausible tentative connection. | Question proposes an observable test, such as repeated rolls. | Do not require energy vocabulary; accept labels or a scribe to distinguish language access from understanding.
samples: Faster motion may scatter more pieces; repeat both speeds to check. | My guess proves every future result.

stem: A child says, "The next cup roll will go farther." Label this as observed or expected.
answer: Expected; that future trial has not happened.
steps: Label expected. | Distinguish future prediction from observation.
samples: Expected; it has not happened. | Observed; the child said it.

stem: Two setups use the same marble and surface. Setup A changes speed and cup size. Setup B changes only speed. Cross out the extra change.
answer: Cup size in A; B isolates speed.
steps: Cross out cup size. | Either speed or cup size could cause the result in A.
samples: Keep cup size fixed to isolate speed. | Changing both makes it fairer.

stem: Watch the repeated marble rolls. Record whether the comparison stayed fair. Note any extra change and one observed effect.
answer: Honestly record conditions and effects, including accidental changes.
steps: Check marble, cup, surface, cup start and contact alignment. | Record a visible effect; no invented measurement.
samples: The same cup start was kept; one off-center hit needs flagging. | Different cups prove speed matters.

stem: A ring rolls into a lid. Plan a fair test of faster and slower ring rolls. Show what changes, what stays, and what you watch.
answer: Change speed; keep ring, lid, surface, lid start and contact arrangement fixed. Repeat both speeds and observe lid motion.
steps: Vary speed only. | Keep ring, lid, surface, target start and contact fixed. | Observe lid motion and repeat both speeds. | Accept concise notes or labeled drawing; a language gap is not a control error.
samples: Change speed; keep the ring, lid, surface, start and contact fixed. Repeat and watch travel. | Use a different lid for each speed.

stem: A slower roll uses one cup. A faster roll uses a larger cup. Cross out the change that hides the speed effect.
answer: Cross out larger cup; keep the receiver unchanged.
steps: Identify cup change. | Retain the same cup for both speeds.
samples: Use the same cup to isolate speed. | Keep changing cups.

stem: Invented for practice. A pencil starts at ruler mark 2 and ends at 7 centimeters. Show its travel by counting intervals.
answer: Five one-centimeter intervals; travel is 5 centimeters.
steps: Count intervals 2 to 3, 3 to 4, 4 to 5, 5 to 6 and 6 to 7. | Record 5 centimeters, not endpoint 7.
samples: Five intervals, so 5 centimeters. | The pencil travels 7 centimeters.

stem: Invented for practice. A ribbon is 5 centimeters long. Place one mark for its length on a labeled line plot.
answer: One mark above 5, axis labeled length in centimeters.
steps: Use equal whole-centimeter intervals. | Place one mark at 5; label length in centimeters.
samples: One mark at 5 on a length-in-centimeters axis. | The axis measures energy in centimeters.

stem: Record each cup trial in the table. Give speed, trial label and travel in centimeters. Keep unreadable trials visible.
answer: Six trial rows with units and honest unclear readings.
steps: Each row has speed and trial label. | Nearest whole-centimeter mark; less than one centimeter is not zero. | Repeat an unclear reading once; keep both entries.
samples: S1: 3 centimeters; S2: unreadable; S2 repeat: 4 centimeters; other trials retained. | Erase the awkward result and invent a matching one.

stem: The washer starts at 6 centimeters and stops at 15 centimeters. Another trial moves it 9 centimeters. Record both travel distances with units. Plot both trials on a labeled line plot.
answer: 9 centimeters twice; two stacked marks at 9, axis labeled distance in centimeters.
steps: 15 minus 6 gives 9 centimeters. | Second travel is 9 centimeters. | Two marks above 9 on a distance-in-centimeters axis. | Allow enlarged axes or a scribe for motor and language access.
samples: 9 centimeters and 9 centimeters; two marks at 9 on a labeled distance axis. | First travel is 15 centimeters.

stem: Review the pencil record from day 3. Count the spaces from 2 to 7 centimeters. Label what the ruler measures.
answer: 5 centimeters of distance.
steps: Count five intervals. | Label distance in centimeters.
samples: Five centimeters of travel. | The endpoint 7 is the travel.

stem: Choose one row from our cup table. Add its mark to the class plot. Label one observed cup change.
answer: Match the row to its mark; describe observed cup motion.
steps: Match distance and speed series. | Keep equal intervals and speed labels. | Describe an effect, never energy units.
samples: The S1 mark matches its row; cup motion changed after contact. | The cup moved centimeters of energy.

stem: What happens repeatedly after our faster marble rolls? What might that tell us about the moving marble?
answer: If controlled repeats separate consistently, greater effects support more motion energy in the faster marble.
steps: Check actual records first. | Repeated greater controlled effects support more motion energy. | Overlap calls for further trials, not altered records.
samples: Each faster effect is farther, supporting more motion energy. | The same marble has equal energy at both speeds.

stem: The same disk hits the same target. What repeated pattern connects its speed and motion energy? Use both displays.
answer: Both displays show each faster trial moving the target farther; faster disk motion has more energy.
steps: Table and plot: slower 2, 3, 2; faster 7, 8, 7 centimeters. | Every faster effect exceeds every slower effect. | Connect speed to more motion energy. | Accept concise labels or a scribe for language access.
samples: Both displays show every faster trial farther; faster motion has more energy. | The same disk has equal energy at both speeds.

stem: Review our marble record. Point to the repeated speed difference and label what centimeters measure.
answer: Each faster effect is farther in the separating record; centimeters measure travel.
steps: Use repeats at both speeds. | Distinguish distance from energy. | Same object can have different motion energy.
samples: All faster effects are farther; centimeters label travel. | Same marble means equal energy.

stem: Use our marble observations to explain aloud why cup motion supports your claim. Point to repeated evidence.
answer: Faster marble motion has more energy available to pass to the cup; repeated greater effects support this.
steps: Claim about the same marble at two speeds. | Repeated controlled effects as evidence. | Energy passes at contact and changes cup motion; distance is not energy units.
samples: Faster marble motion has more energy. Repeated faster rolls move the cup farther. Energy passes to the cup at contact. That changes motion and supports the claim. | Fast means fast; evidence is unnecessary.

stem: Write three short evidence notes: repeated outcomes, a fixed condition, and what the cup did.
answer: Three relevant notes, not a complete written explanation.
steps: Name repeated outcomes. | Name a fixed condition. | Describe cup motion without energy units.
samples: All faster effects farther; same cup start; cup moved after contact. | The cup traveled centimeters of energy.

stem: Explain which roll had more motion energy. Use the trials and explain why target motion supports your idea.
answer: Faster cylinder motion has more energy; all three faster effects exceed all three slower effects; transfer changes target motion.
steps: Identify faster roll. | Cite repeats at both speeds. | Explain energy passing to the target, changing its motion; greater controlled effects support more available energy. | Allow a scribe for the independent child's own explanation.
samples: The faster roll has more motion energy. Every faster effect is farther. Energy passes to the target at contact and changes its motion. Greater controlled effects support more available energy. | Same cylinder means equal energy.

stem: Review day 5's marble record. Point to the repeated effects supporting more motion energy at faster speed.
answer: Use separating outcomes at both speeds, conditions fixed.
steps: Cite repeated effects at both speeds. | Same object does not imply equal energy when speed differs.
samples: All faster effects were farther in this record. | One marble always has equal motion energy.

stem: Invented for practice: the same toy tire hits the same index card. Each speed has three trials. Every faster trial moves the card farther. Choose the explanation using transfer.
answer: Statement A connects energy passing to the card with its changed motion.
steps: A: Faster tire motion has more energy available to transfer at contact; that changes card motion. | B: Faster tire motion has more energy because that is what faster means. | A supplies a mechanism; B restates the claim.
samples: A connects transfer to card motion, supported by repeated greater effects. | B supplies evidence by repeating faster.

stem: Match evidence strips to complete statements. Mark which observation supports the speed claim. Add a short evidence note.
answer: Greater repeated faster effects support the speed claim; fixed conditions support comparability; motion after contact supports transfer.
steps: Match independently first. | Repeated outcomes support the speed claim. | Fixed conditions support fairness, not energy quantity. | Keep the note brief; do not rewrite an explanation.
samples: Every faster trial farther supports the claim; same tire supports fairness. | Same tire proves equal energy.

stem: Strengthen this explanation with trial evidence and a transfer reason.
answer: Add repeated greater tube motion and energy passing from hoop to tube, changing tube motion.
steps: Cite repeated farther tube motion at faster speed. | Explain transfer at contact changing tube motion. | Link controlled greater effects to more available motion energy, never energy units of distance. | Allow a scribe for the child's own independent explanation.
samples: Repeated faster rolls moved the same tube farther. Energy passed to the tube, changing its motion. Greater controlled effects support more available energy. | The same hoop always has equal energy.
